node.label: Laurel Thatcher Ulrich
node.date_label: Good Wives (1982) · A Midwife's Tale (1990) · The Age of Homespun (2001)
node.description: In A Midwife's Tale (1990), Laurel Thatcher Ulrich argues that women's work and exchanges were central to the organization of an early American community. By connecting Martha Ballard's terse diary entries with other records, she reconstructs relationships that a record of public events would miss. Good Wives (1982) explains how a wife acting as a deputy husband could undertake men's work without overturning patriarchal authority. Nancy F. Cott's 1983 review praised its recovery of women's lives from contextual records. A Midwife's Tale won the 1991 Pulitzer Prize and became a collaborative PBS documentary. The Age of Homespun (2001) extends Ulrich's inquiry to textiles, social relationships and nostalgic versions of the national past. Grace Lees-Maffei's 2002 review praised that book while questioning its reception as a novel method: design historians had long treated objects as historical evidence.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Good Wives: Image and Reality in the Lives of Women in Northern New England, 1650–1750 (1982); A Midwife's Tale: The Life of Martha Ballard, Based on Her Diary, 1785–1812 (1990); The Age of Homespun: Objects and Stories in the Creation of an American Myth (2001).
node.scope_note: Selected interview passages, publisher descriptions, a complete submitted book review, Cott's first review page, Lepore's first-page acknowledgments read. Ulrich's monographs, Cott's continuation, Lepore's full essay and Demos's review unread; documentary not watched.

proposed_edges.relationship: Cott's 1983 review of Good Wives (1982) credits Ulrich's reconstruction of women through contextual records and finds the deputy-husband role useful for explaining work across gender boundaries within patriarchal authority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher's first-page preview, printed p. 173, right column, review's opening three paragraphs. Short anchors: 'eliminates the excuse' and 'particularly useful'. This is a documented published assessment, not a claim of personal mentorship or comprehensive agreement. Read only p. 173; continuation p. 174 and Good Wives itself unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Good Wives (1982) explains how women could undertake men's work as deputy husbands while their authority remained contingent on household relationships.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cott, first-page review preview, printed p. 173, second paragraph distinguishes task from position and crossing gender boundaries from independence. The author's 2015 interview, answer beginning 'It's important to know that my first book', describes the relation between Good Wives and the later diary research. Cott is a named scholarly reader; the 1982 book body is unread. This contribution to the existing broad gender field does not subsume women's history into a single theory.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pearsall and Sword’s 2009 AHA biography credits A Midwife’s Tale (1990) with using one woman’s diary to reconstruct her community and reassess wider historical narratives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sarah Pearsall and Kirsten Sword, AHA presidential biography (2009), Old Diary, paragraphs beginning A Midwife’s Tale showed scholars and Laurel’s painstaking reconstruction, read on the AHA’s site. These named scholars explain how reconstructing one woman’s life changes broader interpretations. The endpoint micro is labelled Microhistory / everyday life: this is a contribution to its broad everyday-life remit, not a claim that the biographers use the word microhistory or identify an Italian/German school affiliation. The library listing is removed as evidence; the monograph itself remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Age of Homespun (2001) interprets the making, use and preservation of textiles as evidence of social relationships and identity, contributing to material-culture history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher's Book Description, final paragraph; Lees-Maffei's submitted review, PDF p. 1, opening and discussion of practical knowledge of spinning, and p. 2, closing assessment. Review anchors: 'analysis of its objects' and 'path well trodden'. Her criticism of novelty is retained in the node. Book body unread; no claim that Ulrich invented the study of objects. Only scholarly method is summarized.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Age of Homespun (2001) examines how household production became a nostalgic account of the American past and uses object histories to question that account.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher's Book Description, second paragraph; Lees-Maffei's submitted review, PDF p. 1, paragraph beginning 'The Introduction goes on', citing the book's p. 36 on a historical narrative becoming orthodoxy. This relationship concerns the construction of retrospective national memory, distinct from the material-evidence method in the consumption edge. Only description/review read; no debt to Halbwachs or Nora asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ulrich collaborated in the documentary adaptation of A Midwife's Tale (book 1990; PBS broadcast 1998), making the process of reconstructing history from records part of its public presentation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: PBS Film Description, paragraph beginning 'For five years', and Credits explicitly name Ulrich, Laurie Kahn-Leavitt and Richard P. Rogers and describe showing the historian's research. The CV, PDF pp. 4–5, PUBLIC HISTORY PROJECTS, identifies her as narrator and consultant and separately as DoHistory advisor. Claim is collaboration and interpretive presentation, not sole authorship or evidence from viewing the film. The displayed broadcast date is 19 January 1998.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her American Historical Review review (June 1991) of Merchant's Ecological Revolutions (1989), Ulrich notes its effort to connect ecology and feminism and praises its concrete accounts of farming, but finds its attempts to map long-term change 'often tenuous', points to 'a similar casualness about causality', and says Merchant is more comfortable contrasting fixed types than delineating causal and chronological sequences.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's own first-page preview (Oxford Academic, AHR 96.3, June 1991, p. 945; the review begins in the lower left column and runs onto p. 946). Landing metadata: reviewer Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, University of New Hampshire. Phrases seen: 'Readers who know Carolyn Merchant's first book, The Death of Nature ... will find this new study both familiar and surprising—familiar in its effort to connect ecology and feminism'; 'Merchant has the gift of being able to make plain dirt interesting'; 'The chapters that follow are eclectic, even at some points eccentric, ranging from rich descriptions of objects, habitats, and processes to sometimes convincing, often tenuous, attempts to map long-term change'; 'Merchant is clearly more comfortable contrasting fixed types—corn mothers versus Puritan fathers, subsistence farmers versus market agriculturists—than in delineating causal and chronological sequences'; 'A similar casualness about causality makes it difficult to understand how the descendants of the witch-hunting Puritans ... became the benign subsistence farmers'; on Merchant's p. 86, 'Actually, the pathogens, borne by transient fishermen and traders, came first'; and, more favourably, 'The descriptions of subsistence farming are more convincing.' Limits: p. 946 (the end of the review and any final judgement) unread; the claim is limited to the criticisms and praise on p. 945. The review engages Merchant's argument directly; it is not a citation. Merchant's book itself not reread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: A Midwife's Tale (1990) reshaped women's history by challenging both accounts of an early golden age and narratives of a political void before feminism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pearsall and Sword identify competing narratives displaced by the book; no claim about particular scholars.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ulrich's A Midwife's Tale (1990) inspired the documentary and DoHistory website, which Pearsall and Sword identify as an influential experiment in digital history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The authors describe a book–film–website sequence and participatory access to primary sources; credit remains collaborative.

proposed_edges.relationship: Heasim Sul's 2015 survey of microhistory in the history of medicine names A Midwife's Tale (1990), with works by Ruggiero and Cressy, as clearly demonstrating microhistory's methods and revealing the complexity of early modern medicine and personal relationships.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal-published English abstract, not the Korean article body. Sul explicitly includes Ulrich among three studies illustrating medical microhistory and the complexity of early modern medicine. This supports a bounded field contribution, not personal influence on Sul or a claim to have founded the field.
